description_full: Edwards Lifesciences Corporation provides products and technologies to treat advanced cardiovascular diseases in the United States, Europe, Japan, and internationally. It offers transcatheter heart valve replacement products for minimally invasive replacement of aortic heart valves under the Edwards SAPIEN family of valves system; and transcatheter heart valve repair and replacement products to treat mitral and tricuspid valve diseases under the PASCAL and EVOQUE brands. The company also provides surgical structural heart solutions, such as aortic surgical valve under the INSPIRIS brand name; INSPIRIS RESILIA aortic valve, which offers RESILIA tissue and VFit technology; KONECT RESILIA, a pre-assembled tissue valve conduit for complex combined procedures; and MITRIS RESILIA valve. It distributes its products through a direct sales force and independent distributors. Edwards Lifesciences Corporation was founded in 1958 and is headquartered in Irvine, California.

financial_summary: Edwards Lifesciences Corporatio is a large-cap healthcare business with a $61.6B market cap on $6.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 25% against a 9% cost of capital — a 15-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 75% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.3B in free cash flow — roughly 22 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.49× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 62× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.5%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 21% operating margin runs 21pp above the Healthcare median (0%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.38x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 462 companies in the universe; the top four hold 35% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 1% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.97, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.34 vs 5y 0.96), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $300.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash, 47% in the 2022 bear market and 32% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $51.00 (margin of safety -110%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 24%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $41.61 to $64.32 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Healthcare peers: P/E 62.3 vs 26.2, EV/EBITDA 27.2 vs 15.5 and P/FCF 46.2 vs 23.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 38% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 27 covering analysts target $113 on average, 6% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 25% clears the cost of capital of 9.4% by 15pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.30).
It runs a 75% gross margin and converts 22% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.49x.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 17.8% of revenue on R&D and 2.6% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $3.6B (6% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 13.6, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 286 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.1% over 3 years, 6.7% over 5 years and 9.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 24% of profits supports about 5.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 15.6% a year over five years.
Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (4.3% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 26, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 3.7% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 95%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (14 sales, net $11.8M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.5% (1.5% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 1.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 16,000 employees, each generates about $379K of revenue, in line with the Healthcare median, and revenue has grown 10.0% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $83K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.8M (10x revenue per employee).
